title: Flooding or accidental leakage of cargo pumproom bilges
plain: Can the officers pump out a flooded cargo pumproom, and are the bilge arrangements in good order?
why: A flooded pumproom must be pumped out quickly and without pollution, even if nobody can safely go inside.
checks: Company procedure for draining the pumproom bilges
Remote controls for bilge pump and valves on the upper deck
Valves that must stay open are set correctly and marked
Officer can explain the line-up to a slop or cargo tank
Test records and Oil Record Book Part II entries
ready: Procedure for draining pumproom bilges
Emergency response plan for pumproom flooding
Oil Record Book Part II with bilge disposals entered
Records of periodic tests of the bilge arrangements
Valves and remote controls labelled with their purpose
traps: No procedure or no pumproom flooding emergency plan
Officer cannot explain the remote pumping line-up
Remote controls missing, defective or officer does not know where they are
Steam or condensate valves needed for pumping left shut
No evidence of periodic testing of the arrangements
Bilge pump defective, or bilge disposal not in the ORB Part II
say: Our SMS has a procedure for draining the pumproom bilges to a slop or cargo tank. I can show you the remote controls for the bilge pump and valves on the upper deck, and they are tested periodically. Any disposal of bilge contents is recorded in the Oil Record Book Part II.

practice.q: If the pumproom floods, how would you pump it out?
a: Use remote controls from the upper deck, not by entering
Line up bilge pump to slop or cargo tank
Check required valves are open, including steam and condensate
Follow the pumproom flooding emergency plan

practice.q: How do you know the arrangement works?
a: Periodic tests are done and recorded
Valves and controls are marked with purpose
Defects are reported and repaired

tip: Walk the remote controls on the upper deck before the inspection and check every label is readable.

title: Cargo system overboard and sea suction valves
plain: Are sea and overboard valves checked closed and secured before cargo transfer, and is leakage monitored and tested?
why: A leaking or open sea valve can send cargo straight overboard.
checks: Company procedure for sea valves, ballasting through sea suction and line displacement
Valves closed and secured with lock-out/tag-out, in-line blanks fitted
Records of checks before each cargo transfer
Leak detection gauge between inboard and outboard valves
Records of integrity tests between dry-dockings
ready: Procedure with test pressure limit stated
Bridge or cargo logbook entries showing valves checked closed and secured
Records of leakage checks and dry-dock integrity tests
Pressure/vacuum gauge in good order
Anti-pollution notices at each valve and at the pump operating position
traps: Valves not fully closed or not locked before cargo transfer
No lock-out/tag-out, or no marking on hydraulic valves
In-line blanks not inserted where provided
No record of pre-transfer checks or leakage checks
Gauge shows leakage, damaged, or only a pressure gauge fitted
Notice 'start pump before opening sea suction' missing
say: Before every cargo transfer we check the sea and overboard valves are closed and secured, and we record it in the logbook. Where leak monitoring is fitted we read the gauge and note any leakage. Integrity tests are done between dry-dockings, within the test pressure in our procedure.

practice.q: How do you secure the sea valves during cargo operations?
a: Closed and secured with lock-out/tag-out
In-line blanks inserted where fitted
Hydraulic valves clearly marked as to stay closed
Check recorded before transfer

practice.q: How do you start ballasting through a sea suction?
a: Start the pump before opening the sea suction
Vent the pump so no oil escapes overboard
Watch the gauge for vacuum or leakage

tip: Read the leak gauge yourself during the walk-round so you can tell the inspector the actual reading.
refs: OCIMF/ICS Prevention of Oil Spillages through Cargo Pumproom Sea Valves

title: Bunker pipeline system pressure testing
plain: Do officers know how the bunker pipelines are inspected and pressure tested, and are the tests recorded?
why: Regular testing finds weak points and leaks before they cause a bunker spill.
checks: Company procedure for inspection and pressure testing of the bunker line
Test records: date, pressure, method and test liquid
Pipelines marked with date and pressure of last test
Records of liquid disposal after testing
Relief valve and tank level alarm test records
ready: Procedure covering equipment, frequency, method, pressure, disposal, records
Test records, possibly in the maintenance plan
Records of relief valve and level alarm tests
Records showing disposal of the test liquid
Test date and pressure marked on the lines
traps: No procedure, or officer cannot explain the test method
No test records or no disposal records
Lines not marked with last test date and pressure
Not tested to 100 percent of MAWP in last 12 months
Not tested to 150 percent of MAWP twice in last 5 years
Tested with air or inert gas instead of a suitable liquid
say: Our procedure covers what is tested, how often, the method, the test pressure and where the test liquid goes. Tests are hydrostatic, never with air or gas. Each line is marked with the last test date and pressure, and records are in the maintenance plan.

practice.q: How do you pressure test the bunker lines?
a: Hydrostatic test with a suitable liquid
Pressure as set in company procedure, based on MAWP
Record date, pressure, method and medium

practice.q: What if the drawings do not show MAWP?
a: Use relief valve set pressure
Or maximum pump discharge pressure including hydraulic shock if no relief valve

tip: Check the line markings on deck match the dates in your maintenance records.
refs: USCG Marine Safety Manual Vol II

title: Ballast water management system (BWMS)
plain: Do officers know how to run the BWMS safely, and is it working and used as per procedure and maker's manual?
why: The system can create toxic gas or chemical hazards, and a faulty or bypassed unit means ballast is not properly treated.
checks: Company procedure and maker's operation and safety manual
Control panel: system operational, no faults or alarms
Self-monitoring data from the last ballast operation
Unit intact, not modified or bypassed
Chemical stock, storage and handling if used
ready: Procedure naming who supervises and who may operate the BWMS
Maker's operation and safety manual
Maintenance and inspection records in the plan
Operation records for each ballast operation
Enclosed space procedure posted for the BWMS room
traps: No procedure covering hazards, chemicals, by-products and failure actions
Officer does not know hazards or what to do if the BWMS fails
No maintenance records in the plan or no operation records
Pumps, filters or back-flush not working
Self-monitoring data shows it did not work properly last time
BWMS modified or bypassed, or not enough chemicals, or poor chemical storage
say: Our SMS says who supervises and who may operate the BWMS, and lists the hazards and controls. We follow the maker's manual, keep operation and maintenance records, and know the actions if it fails. Chemicals are stored and handled as per the procedure.

practice.q: What hazards does the BWMS present?
a: Toxic or flammable gas, such as hydrogen from electrolysis systems
Chemicals used for disinfection or neutralisation
Treatment room treated as an enclosed space

practice.q: What do you do if the BWMS fails?
a: Follow the failure actions in the company procedure
Know these actions before the operation starts
Record the failure

tip: Check the BWMS room entry notice matches your enclosed space entry procedure, or you collect a second observation under 5.5.1.

title: Main deck oil or chemical spill clean up equipment
plain: Do crew know how to clean up small spills on deck, and is the equipment ready, in good order and used well?
why: A small deck spill must be contained and cleaned quickly so it never reaches the sea or becomes a fire risk.
checks: SOPEP or SMPEP and company procedure for deck spills
Inventory of spill equipment and inspection records
Equipment at the manifold, quantities match the inventory
Dump valves or other disposal means aft on both sides
Portable pump demonstrated, and a rating asked about equipment and PPE
ready: SOPEP or SMPEP and spill procedure
Inventory kept by a designated officer, with periodic checks
Instructions for safe use including PPE
Non-sparking scoops, shovels, buckets, sorbents, scupper plugs
Portable pump bonded, fixed down, with air ready
traps: No inventory, or inspection records missing, or quantities differ from the inventory
Equipment missing at the manifold or in short supply
Scoops or buckets not non-sparking
Portable pump not bonded, not secured, no air, or hose through a sighting port
Dump valves would not drain, or limits not posted
No spill tank or drip tray under each manifold connection, or an unbonded plastic tray
say: Our spill equipment is kept at the manifold and listed in an inventory kept by a designated officer, with periodic inspections. The crew are trained and know the PPE for the cargo carried. The portable pump is bonded and ready, and recovered waste is disposed of as per our procedure.

practice.q: A small spill happens at the manifold. What do you do?
a: Stop the operation and raise the alarm
Contain it with scupper plugs and sorbents
Remove with non-sparking tools and pump, then dispose properly

practice.q: Rating: where is the spill kit and what PPE do you wear?
a: Know the location of the equipment
Use PPE required for the cargo being handled
Know what each item is for

tip: Ratings are asked this question directly, so run a quick spill kit talk with the deck team before the inspection.

title: Disposal of oily water in the forecastle and other internal spaces
plain: Do officers know how to dispose of oily or polluted water collected in the forecastle and similar spaces?
why: Oil from a hydraulic leak in a bilge well must not go overboard and must be traceable.
checks: Company procedure for bilge wells in internal spaces
Records of disposals
Bilge wells in forecastle, pumproom and steering gear
How levels are monitored and how unauthorised discharge is prevented
Pollution notices and secured overboard valves where pumps or ejectors fitted
ready: Procedure listing spaces, minimising waste, monitoring, disposal and records
Disposal records for any past leaks
Notices posted and overboard valves secured
Bilge wells clean and checked
Pump testing in the maintenance plan
traps: No procedure or officer does not know it
Evidence of a leak but no record of how it was disposed of
Disposal arrangements or discharge prevention inadequate
Bilge well with a significant amount of oil or pollutant
Spaces not identified in the procedure
say: Our procedure lists the spaces with bilge wells, how levels are checked and how oily water is disposed of. Every disposal is recorded. Where pumps are fitted, overboard valves are secured and notices are posted.

practice.q: What if you find oily water in the forecastle bilge well?
a: Find and stop the source
Dispose ashore or to a proper tank, never overboard
Record how it was disposed of

practice.q: How do you stop accidental discharge?
a: Overboard valves secured
Pollution notices posted
Regular inspection of bilge levels

tip: Look in the forecastle bilge well the day before: a small hydraulic leak with no record is a classic finding.

title: Emergency arrangements to pump out the machinery space bilges
plain: Do engineers know how to pump out a flooded engine room, and are valves marked and in good order?
why: In a flooding the engine room must be pumped out fast, without misuse of the emergency suction for daily bilges.
checks: Company procedure for emergency bilge pumping
Emergency bilge suction valve accessible and clearly marked
Valves marked, and which pump to start is shown
Warning signs on emergency overboard valves, and seals
Engineer explains sequence for sea water pipe failure and other flooding
ready: Procedure and machinery space flooding emergency plan
Marked valves and suction, pump indication
Warning notices posted
Numbered easily breakable seals recorded in log or ORB Part I
Valves free to operate, not seized
traps: No procedure or no flooding emergency plan
Engineer cannot explain the valve and pump sequence
Emergency suction not accessible or not marked
No warning notice on emergency overboard valve
Seals missing, not as procedure, or not easily breakable
Evidence emergency discharge used for daily bilge disposal
say: Our procedure covers the bilge pumps, direct suctions and the emergency bilge suction. Valves are marked and sealed with numbered breakable seals recorded in the log. I can explain the sequence for a sea water pipe failure and for other flooding. The emergency line is never used for daily bilges.

practice.q: The engine room is flooding. What do you do?
a: Follow the flooding emergency plan and procedure
Line up the emergency bilge suction and overboard valves in the sequence in the procedure
Start the pump marked for the emergency suction
Break the seal and inform the bridge

practice.q: Can you use this line for daily bilge disposal?
a: No, emergency use only
MARPOL exceptions: to secure ship safety or save life, or after damage to ship or equipment
Seal numbers recorded

tip: Know which pump serves the emergency suction and be able to point to it without looking at the drawing.

title: Incinerator operation
plain: Do engineers know how to use the incinerator safely and legally, and is it in good order?
why: Burning the wrong waste breaks MARPOL and creates fire, fume and health risks.
checks: Company procedure and risk assessment for safe incinerator use
Operating instructions posted at the controls
List of items not to be incinerated posted in the space
Loading chute interlocks working and not bypassed
Engineer explains PPE, loading, emergency stop and prohibited items
ready: Procedure and risk assessment
Operation and maintenance manual
Prohibited items list posted
Separated waste stored for disposal ashore
Clean incinerator space with no waste piled up
traps: No procedure or no risk assessment
Engineer unsure about PPE, loading, prohibited items or failure actions
Incinerator out of service or defective; no instructions or prohibited list posted
Overheated casing, fume leaks, or oil dripping around casing; interlocks defective or bypassed
Burning in places or times where MARPOL, local rules or company procedure forbid it
Waste left to pile up around the space
say: Our procedure says who may use the incinerator, when it must not be used, and what may and may not be burned. The risk assessment covers the chute interlocks. Instructions and the prohibited items list are posted at the incinerator, and I know the PPE and emergency stop.

practice.q: What must you never burn in the incinerator?
a: Cargo residues and PCBs
Exhaust gas cleaning residues
PVC unless in a type-approved incinerator
Items on the posted prohibited list

practice.q: When is incinerator use not allowed?
a: Where MARPOL, local rules or company procedure forbid it
Sludge in ports, harbours and estuaries

tip: Test that the interlock really prevents the chute opening while the furnace is hot, as far as possible with the unit stopped.

title: Oil filtering equipment
plain: Do engineers know how to use the oily water separator, and is it working, sealed and used per MARPOL?
why: Bilge discharges must stay within MARPOL limits, and tampering or misuse means illegal pollution.
checks: Company procedure for use of the oil filtering equipment
Overboard valve closed, secured and sealed with a warning sign
Flanges and connections sealed with no signs of tampering
15 ppm alarm calibration certificate
Engineer demonstrates alarm, automatic stopping device and recorder using the test facility
ready: Procedure and maker's manuals
Bilge alarm calibration certificate
Maintenance records in the plan
Oil Record Book Part I with any out-of-service entries
Bilge alarm data kept as the procedure says
traps: No procedure, or officer cannot explain the restrictions and fault actions
Alarm not calibrated within five years or the maker's period if shorter
Overboard valve open, unsealed or no warning sign
Signs of tampering or unsealed flanges; equipment defective, or no maintenance records
Engineer cannot demonstrate alarm, stopping device or recorder
Out of service with no Oil Record Book Part I entry
say: Our procedure says who may use the separator and when overboard discharge is allowed. The overboard valve is locked and sealed, with the key held as per procedure. I can demonstrate the alarm, stopping device and recorder, and any breakdown is entered in the ORB Part I.

practice.q: The separator breaks down. What do you do?
a: Stop use and follow the company procedure
Record time out of service and returned in ORB Part I
Retain bilges onboard or land ashore

practice.q: What if you find a flange or pipe has been tampered with?
a: Report to Chief Engineer and Master
Follow the company procedure
Do not use the equipment

tip: Practise the test facility demonstration before the inspector asks, including the recorder print-out.

title: Oil discharge monitoring and control system (ODME)
plain: Do officers know how to use the ODME, and is it working and used as per procedure, maker and MARPOL?
why: ODME keeps discharges from cargo and ballast spaces within MARPOL limits and records them.
checks: Company procedure for ODME use and authorisation
Control panel with no faults or alarms
Printout or stored data legible and available
Speed, position and GMT time inputs correct
Records for any manual-mode discharge and failures
ready: Procedure and maker's manuals
Maintenance and test records
ODME printouts or downloadable data
Oil Record Book Part II and bridge logbook
Written shore approval if any manual mode discharge was done
traps: No procedure or officer does not know manual mode and fault actions
System defective, modified or extra connections added
Maintenance and testing not as maker and procedure say
Manual mode discharge with no shore management approval
Printout illegible or data not available
Out of service with no ORB Part II entry
say: Our procedure covers who may operate ODME, checks before and after discharge, lookouts and what to do if it fails. We keep the printouts and enter everything in the ORB Part II. Manual mode is never used without approval from shore management.

practice.q: ODME fails during discharge. What do you do?
a: Stop the discharge
Record the defect in ORB Part II
Inform shore management and get approval before any manual mode

practice.q: What if the lookout sees a slick astern?
a: Stop the discharge immediately
Inform the bridge and Master
Follow the pollution emergency plan

tip: Check the speed, position and GMT time on the ODME panel are correct before the inspector looks.

title: Security threat and risk assessment during passage planning
plain: Is security risk assessed in voyage planning, and does the passage plan carry security information for each leg?
why: Piracy and armed robbery risks must be planned for before entering an area, not met by surprise.
checks: Security charts and BMP or regional guidance on the bridge
Passage plan and security risk assessment for a recent voyage
Security notes on each leg, reporting points, speed, bridge manning
Review of the assessment before entering an increased risk area
Bridge security cards or checklists
ready: UKHO or equivalent security charts
BMP and regional guidance such as ReCAAP
Passage plan, appraisal form and risk assessment for a completed voyage
Company advice on routeing, speed, waiting areas
Bridge logbook and bridge security cards
traps: Security charts or BMP publications missing
No security risk assessment for a recent voyage
Assessment lists no ship protection measures where needed
No company routeing guidance for a high-risk transit
Assessment not reviewed or plan not updated before entering the area
Passage plan has no security information for each leg; bridge security cards missing
say: We do a ship-specific threat and risk assessment for every voyage, using current security charts, BMP and company guidance. The passage plan marks security levels, reporting points, extra lookouts and speed. We review it before entering an increased risk area. The security plan is confidential, so I will describe it only in general.

practice.q: What security information is in your passage plan?
a: Reporting points such as entering a VRA
Bridge manning, speed and day or night transit
Security level changes and hardening points

practice.q: When do you review the risk assessment?
a: Before entering an area needing higher vigilance
Update the passage plan if needed

tip: If the company tells you not to report to a VRA, annotate the plan so the reporting points are shown as not to be used.

title: Vessel hardening
plain: Do officers know how to harden the ship for areas of increased security risk, and is there a Vessel Hardening Plan?
why: Hardening makes it much harder to board the ship, but it must not block escape routes or lifesaving gear.
checks: Company procedure and ship-specific Vessel Hardening Plan (VHP)
VHP lists materials and quantities needed
Inventory of hardening materials against stock onboard
Maintenance records for water cannons, CCTV, cameras
Security officer explains the plan, LSA and FFA stay accessible
ready: Vessel Hardening Plan, which can sit in the SSP
Inventory of hardening materials
Inspection and maintenance records for security equipment
Records of past implementation such as logs, work plans, photographs
Safety guidance for rigging razor wire and working near the ship's side
traps: No procedure or no VHP
VHP not ship-specific, or lacks materials list and quantities
No inventory, or inventory does not match actual stock
No maintenance records for security equipment
No record that the VHP was implemented before the area
Security officer not familiar with the plan
say: Our VHP is specific to this ship and lists the materials and quantities needed. We keep an inventory and maintain the security equipment. When hardened, lifeboats, life rafts and firefighting gear stay clear. The security plan is confidential, so I can show the cover and review date.

practice.q: What does the VHP include?
a: Ship-specific measures and materials list with quantities
Inventory and when materials are kept onboard
Maintenance of security equipment
Safety guidance for rigging

practice.q: What must hardening not interfere with?
a: Escape routes
Lifesaving appliances and firefighting equipment
Response to non-security emergencies

tip: Count the hardening materials against the inventory before the inspection, since a mismatch is easy to spot.

title: Controlling access to the vessel
plain: Do crew control who comes onboard in port and make sure visitors know the hazards and safety rules?
why: Unchecked visitors are a security risk, and visitors who do not know the hazards are a safety risk.
checks: Gangway watch continuous and watchman knows the procedure
Visitor photo ID, passes, log, escort to accommodation
Notice board at the gangway with warnings
Visitor information card or briefing on hazards and rules
Deck patrols for unauthorised access points such as hawse pipes and mooring ropes
ready: Access control procedure, in or outside the SSP
Visitor log with entries in and out
Visitor passes and information cards
Gangway notice board with warnings in suitable languages
List of approved visitors sent to the terminal, including the SIRE inspector
traps: No continuous gangway watch, or watchman unfamiliar with procedure
No list of approved visitors given to the terminal
No deck patrols, or CCTV not monitored
No photo ID, passes or visitor records
Visitors not escorted or baggage not searched per security level
No notice board, or visitors not briefed on smoking, phones, PPE, cargo hazards, emergency signals, drug and alcohol policy
say: We keep a continuous gangway watch, check photo ID, issue passes and log every visitor. Visitors are escorted and given an information card on hazards, PPE, smoking, phones and emergency signals. We patrol the deck for other access points and gave the terminal our approved visitors list.

practice.q: Gangway watch: what do you do when a visitor arrives?
a: Check photo ID and approved list
Issue a pass and record in log
Brief on hazards, give PPE if needed, and escort

practice.q: What else do you watch besides the gangway?
a: Hawse pipes and mooring ropes
CCTV where fitted
Regular deck patrols

tip: Brief the gangway watchman on exactly what the visitor card says. He is the first person the inspector meets.

title: Ship security reporting and communications
plain: Do the Master and officers know the regional security reporting rules and how the SSAS works, and is it tested?
why: Authorities can only help if they know where you are and your alert system works when needed.
checks: 24-hour contact details of the Company Security Officer, posted
Master and SSO know voluntary reporting procedure for VRAs
SSAS, LRIT and any standalone security comms regularly tested
Officers know where the SSAS buttons are and how it works
Whether VRA reporting was considered in passage planning
ready: CSO name and 24-hour contacts posted
Records of voluntary security reporting
Test records for SSAS and LRIT kept per the SSP
Passage plan marking VRA reporting points
Annotations if company told you not to report
traps: Officer does not know the CSO 24-hour contacts, or not posted
Master or SSO not familiar with VRA reporting procedure
No evidence VRA participation considered in planning
Company required reporting but no reports made; no records of regular SSAS or LRIT testing
Officer cannot explain purpose and operation of SSAS or LRIT
Security communication equipment defective
say: The CSO name and 24-hour contacts are posted on the bridge. We consider VRA reporting at passage planning and report as our procedure requires. SSAS and LRIT are tested regularly and I know where the activation buttons are.

practice.q: Where are the SSAS buttons and what do they do?
a: Know all locations
Send a covert alert to company and authorities
Used in a real security threat, not casually

practice.q: How do you report in a VRA?
a: Register and report to the centre as company procedure says
Continue reports while transiting
Or annotate plan if company says not to report

tip: The inspector will not ask you for equipment details, so know purpose and operation, not just that tests are done.

title: Ship Security Officer (SSO)
plain: Does the SSO hold a valid certificate, understand the role, and are security records for port calls kept?
why: A trained SSO and proper port call records show security is actually run onboard, not just written down.
checks: SSO Certificate of Proficiency, valid
SMS names the SSO and lists the role and duties
SSO is a crew member, not an outside consultant
Evidence of regular security inspections by the SSO
Security records for the last 10 port calls, and a rating's knowledge of security procedures
ready: SSO Certificate of Proficiency
SMS section on ship security with SSO duties
Records of regular security inspections
Port call security records for last 10 calls
Contact details of the CSO
traps: SMS does not clearly name the SSO or list the duties
SSO certificate not valid, or SSO is not a crew member
SSO unsure of the SSP purpose, equipment testing, hardening plan, CSO or PFSO role
Rating knows nothing about security procedures or alarm response
No evidence of regular security inspections
Port call security records not kept for the last 10 calls
say: Our SMS names the SSO and lists his duties. I hold a valid Certificate of Proficiency. I carry out regular security inspections and keep the records for the last 10 port calls. The security plan itself is confidential, but I can explain my role and who the CSO is.

practice.q: What are your duties as SSO?
a: Regular security inspections and keeping the SSP up to date
Security awareness, training and drills
Make sure security equipment is tested and maintained
Report incidents and liaise with CSO and PFSO

practice.q: What security records do you keep?
a: Records for the last 10 port calls
Security level and any special measures taken
Inspection and drill records

tip: Brief ratings on the alarm signal and their first action, because the inspector may ask one of them.

title: Cyber security risk management
plain: Do officers know the company cyber procedures, and are they actually in place onboard?
why: A cyber incident can take out navigation, cargo or propulsion systems, so protection and a backup plan must be real.
checks: Company cyber risk procedures and the officer responsible onboard
Register of sensitive IT and OT systems
Locked spaces and secured USB or network ports
Control of admin profiles, passwords, portable media and visitor access
Hard copy cyber contingency plans and IT support contacts
ready: Cyber risk management procedure
Inventory of sensitive IT and OT systems
Approval records for technicians and remote access
Cyber training records
Printed contingency plans and IT support contact details
traps: No procedure, or officer unfamiliar with it
Spaces with sensitive equipment unlocked, or USB ports open
No inventory of IT and OT systems; admin profile held by someone other than a senior officer
Passwords posted at workstations, no password needed, or shared at crew change
Anti-virus or patches not updated, or portable media not scanned offline
No contingency plans or no hard copy; no approval for a technician working on ECDIS or similar
say: Our procedure names who is responsible for cyber risk onboard and lists our IT and OT systems. Only senior officers hold admin profiles, passwords are changed regularly, and USB ports are secured. We have printed contingency plans and IT support contacts if systems are lost.

practice.q: A technician wants to update the ECDIS. What do you do?
a: Get formal approval before access
Supervise the work
Record the access
Check media offline for malware

practice.q: What if you lose GNSS or navigation data?
a: Use the contingency plan
Revert to other position fixing and backups
Inform company IT and shore support

tip: Keep the contingency plan printed at the bridge, not only on a computer that may be the target.
refs: Guidelines on Cyber Security Onboard Ships v4

title: Inert gas system usage on oil tankers
plain: Do officers know the IG procedures, and are cargo tanks kept inert at all times except when gas-free for entry?
why: Inert tanks cannot burn or explode, so any lapse in IG use puts the whole ship at risk.
checks: Company procedure for IG operation
Oxygen in the IG main at 5 percent or less
Tank pressure within the range in the cargo and ballast plan
Oxygen in a random tank less than 8 percent
Cargo, tank cleaning and gas freeing records for last three months
ready: IG procedure and instruction manuals
Cargo and IG records for three months or three voyages
Positive pressure of at least 100 mm WG maintained
Portable oxygen analyser working
Failure action steps known
traps: No procedure, or officer cannot explain IG failure actions
IG not in use when required
Tanks below 100 mm WG, or pressure outside plan values
IG main oxygen over 5 percent, or tank over 8 percent
No periodic oxygen checks
Records missing or show IG not used per procedure
say: We keep cargo tanks inert at all times except when gas-free for entry, with at least 100 mm WG pressure. Oxygen is not more than 5 percent in the IG main and not more than 8 percent in the tanks. If IG fails, we stop discharge, close the deck isolating valve, open the vent and repair.

practice.q: What do you do if the IG system fails?
a: Stop cargo and ballast discharge from inerted tanks
Close the IG deck isolating valve and open the vent valve
Repair immediately and report as required

practice.q: How do you gas free a tank?
a: Purge with IG until hydrocarbon is below the critical dilution line
Never pass through the flammable range

practice.q: How is the inert gas generator used for a Jet A1 cargo?
a: It keeps the cargo tanks inert while the cargo is on board
Use it during discharge, deballasting and tank cleaning
Gas free a tank only when entry is needed

tip: Know the oxygen reading in the main and in a tank at any time, since the inspector may ask you to measure.

title: Crude oil washing operations (COW)
plain: Do officers know how to plan, prepare, run and record COW, and is the COW system in good order?
why: COW is risky: a leak, wet oil or too much oxygen can cause fire or static explosion.
checks: Company procedures and the COW manual
COW plan, checklists, SSSCL and records for current or last operation
Oxygen tested in each tank within 30 minutes before COW and at 8 percent or less
Pressure gauges, lines, machines and heater blanked if outside engine room
Person in charge explains procedures and qualification
ready: COW manual approved and updated for any changes
Completed COW checklists and plan
Records: tanks, machines, start and end times, pattern, pressure, how dry
Evidence line pressure tested and checked for leaks before arrival
Oil Record Book Part II
traps: No procedure, or PIC unfamiliar or not suitably qualified
No approved COW manual, or manual not updated after alterations
Oxygen above 8 percent, or not tested within 30 minutes; records or checklists incomplete
Leaks, defective gauges, or machines turning in tanks not being washed
Source tank not de-bottomed 1 m, slop tank not discharged first
Heater not blanked, hydrants not capped, or washing cycles not as the manual says
say: Our procedure covers roles, planning, checklists and records. We test oxygen in each tank within 30 minutes before washing and it must not be more than 8 percent. We pressure test the line before arrival, use dry crude, blank the heater and watch the line for leaks throughout.

practice.q: What checks before COW starts?
a: Oxygen tested in each tank at 8 percent or less
Line pressure tested and leak checked
Tank cleaning heater blanked, hydrants capped
Checklists completed

practice.q: Why use dry crude?
a: Oil and water mist builds higher static charge
De-bottom source tank by 1 m
Fully discharge slop tank before using it as source

tip: If no COW is planned, the inspector uses your last record, so keep that file complete.

title: Cargo tank isolation from venting system
plain: Do officers know how to control the isolating valves between each tank and the common vent line?
why: A wrongly set isolating valve can over or under pressurise a tank and damage the structure.
checks: Company procedure for isolating valves
Record or display of the current valve status
Valves on deck: correct position, locked, visibly indicated
Records of tests, maintenance and pre-operation checks
Officer explains who may operate them
ready: Isolation procedure
Status record or display at the CCR matching actual valve positions
Locks controlled by the Responsible Officer
Maintenance and pre-operational test records
Authorised personnel list
traps: No procedure or officer unfamiliar with it
Valve incorrectly set, or status differs from the record
No record or display of valve status
Valve not locked, or locks not under the Responsible Officer
No maintenance, testing or pre-operation check records
No clear visual indication of position; anyone allowed to operate valves
say: Each tank isolating valve has a lock under the Responsible Officer's control and a clear position indication. We record valve status in the CCR and check it before every operation. Only authorised persons operate them, and they are tested and maintained.

practice.q: Why isolate a tank, and what must you check before cargo or ballast?
a: Isolating valves are opened before loading, ballasting or discharging that tank
Check status against the record
Locks under the control of the responsible officer

practice.q: What can cause over pressurisation?
a: Incorrect valve setting
Failure of an isolating valve
Casual operation of valves

tip: Walk the deck and compare every valve with the CCR status board before the inspection.

title: Oil cargo tank cleaning procedures
plain: Do deck officers know how to plan, run and record tank cleaning and gas freeing after volatile cargoes?
why: Tank cleaning and gas freeing are among the most hazardous tanker jobs, so every step must be planned and supervised.
checks: Company tank cleaning and gas freeing procedures
Plans, risk assessments, logs and records for recent cleaning
Tank washing done in an inert atmosphere
Supervision by a Responsible Officer and crew briefing
Special methods: steaming, chemicals, slops, purging
ready: Tank washing and gas freeing plans
Risk assessments including any cleaning additives
Logs and records following company procedure
SDS for tank cleaning chemicals
Brief records showing roles and responsibilities explained
traps: No procedure, or officer not familiar; no plans or supporting records for recent cleaning
Plan not followed, or cleaning not carefully planned
Washing without inert gas, including after slop discharge
Hazards or additive risks not assessed, no ALARP measures
No Responsible Officer supervision or crew briefing
Steam into a tank that might be flammable
say: Every tank washing and gas freeing job has a plan and risk assessment, supervised by a Responsible Officer. The crew are briefed on their roles. We wash in an inert atmosphere, steam only inerted or gas-free tanks, and purge before gas freeing. Everything is recorded.

practice.q: When can you steam a tank?
a: Only after inerting, or water washing and gas freeing
Flammable gas not over 10 percent LFL
Avoid steam pressure build-up

practice.q: What do you plan before tank washing?
a: Risk assessment including chemicals
Atmosphere control, supervision and briefing
Slops handling and records

tip: Keep the plan, risk assessment and log for each wash together in one file so records match.

title: Chemical tanker inert gas system usage
plain: Do officers know the IG procedures and use the IG as required by SOLAS, IBC and company procedure?
why: Inert gas prevents fire and explosion, and some chemicals must be inerted or must not be, so using it wrongly is dangerous.
checks: Company IG procedure and instruction manuals
IG oxygen in the main 5 percent or less, tank oxygen under 8 percent
Positive pressure kept in inerted tanks
Records for last three months or three voyages
Officer knows when IG must be used for each cargo and operation
ready: IG procedure covering inerting, padding, discharge, tank cleaning, purging, topping up, failure
Cargo and IG records
Tank oxygen and pressure readings logged
Inerting before discharge continued until oxygen at or below 8 percent
Cargo specifications for oxygen-dependent inhibitors
traps: No procedure, or officer cannot explain IG failure actions
IG not in use when required by SOLAS, IBC or procedure
Tanks not at positive pressure
IG main oxygen over 5 percent, tank over 8 percent; no periodic oxygen checks
Loaded tank inerted before discharge but stopped before oxygen reached 8 percent
Records missing or incomplete
say: Our procedure tells us for each cargo and operation whether IG or nitrogen is needed. We keep positive pressure, check oxygen regularly and record it. Where an oxygen-dependent inhibitor is carried, we only inert before discharge and keep oxygen at or above the minimum the inhibitor needs. If the system fails, we stop discharge and prevent air entering the tanks.

practice.q: How do you know when IG must be used?
a: Check cargo requirements in IBC and SOLAS
Follow cargo specification and company procedure
Special case for oxygen-dependent inhibitors

practice.q: How do you inert a loaded tank before discharge?
a: Introduce inert gas through the distribution system while venting
Continue until oxygen is at or below 8 percent
Vapours vented may be flammable and toxic

tip: Remember the difference between inerting, padding and purging: inspectors like clear definitions.

title: Carriage of inhibited chemical cargoes
plain: Do officers know the procedures for carrying inhibited cargoes and follow them?
why: If the inhibitor fails or is used up, cargo can polymerise, heat up and rupture the tank.
checks: Company procedure for inhibited cargoes
Certificate of protection on board and inhibitor duration not expired
Cargo and adjacent space temperatures monitored at least daily
Oxygen level watched for oxygen-dependent inhibitors, no inerting before loading or in transit
Contingency plan for uncontrolled polymerisation
ready: Procedure covering certificates, temperatures, inerting, vent blockage, nitrogen hose clearing, extra inhibitor, contingency
Certificate of protection for each inhibited cargo
Temperature and inert gas logs
Cargo plans and logbooks
Written contingency plan
traps: No procedure or responsible officer unfamiliar; no certificate of protection on board
Inhibitor effectiveness period expired before discharge
Temperature not monitored daily, or adjacent spaces not monitored
Oxygen not monitored, or cargo inerted before loading or during carriage
Vent system not checked for solid polymer, or blocked
Compressed nitrogen used to clear hoses after loading; no contingency plan for rapid temperature rise
say: We do not load an inhibited cargo without a certificate of protection. We check the inhibitor duration against the voyage, record cargo and adjacent space temperatures daily, watch oxygen for oxygen-dependent inhibitors, and inspect the vents for polymer. We have a contingency plan if temperature rises unexpectedly.

practice.q: The cargo temperature rises with no weather reason. What do you do?
a: Suspect polymerisation
Follow the contingency plan and shipper advice
Add inhibitor or cool adjacent structures
Rapid rise may need jettison

practice.q: Why not bubble nitrogen through an inhibited cargo?
a: Nitrogen depletes dissolved oxygen the inhibitor needs
Do not clear hoses with compressed nitrogen after loading oxygen-dependent cargo
Ask the shipper if unsure

tip: If no inhibited cargo was carried in six months, the inspector will focus on procedures and interviews, so know the plan well.

title: Procedures and Arrangements Manual
plain: Do officers know the P&A Manual, Certificate of Fitness, IBC Code and latest MEPC.2/Circular, and can they get them easily?
why: Cargo planning and MARPOL residue rules depend on these documents, so officers must know what is allowed and how.
checks: P&A Manual available, in English, French or Spanish for international voyages
List of permitted cargoes with the Certificate of Fitness
IBC Code on board
Latest MEPC.2/Circular, issued each year in December
Officer knows stripping quantities for each tank and P&A sections for their duties
ready: P&A Manual in hard copy or digital
Certificate of Fitness with cargo list
IBC Code, chapters 17 and 18 easy to find
Current MEPC.2/Circular
Stripping quantity for each tank known
traps: Officer unfamiliar with P&A Manual, CoF, IBC or Circular
Officer does not know stripping quantities
P&A Manual not readily available, or not in English, French or Spanish
IBC Code or cargo list not readily available
MEPC.2/Circular missing, or not the latest edition
say: The P&A Manual, cargo list, IBC Code and the latest MEPC.2/Circular are all available to officers planning cargo. I know the stripping quantities for each tank and the P&A sections for my duties on tank cleaning, slops and ballasting.

practice.q: What does the P&A Manual tell you?
a: Physical arrangements and operating procedures to comply with MARPOL Annex II
Cargo handling, tank cleaning, slops and ballasting
Stripping quantities for each tank

practice.q: How do you know a cargo is permitted?
a: Check it is on the Certificate of Fitness list
Get full IBC shipping name from shipper
Check latest MEPC.2/Circular for new products

tip: Check you have this year's MEPC.2/Circular after the December reissue, because an old one is a common finding.

title: Chemical tank cleaning procedures
plain: Do deck officers know how to plan, run and record tank cleaning after volatile or toxic cargoes?
why: Tank cleaning exposes crew to toxic and flammable vapours and creates MARPOL slop rules to follow.
checks: Company procedures and P&A Manual
Written tank cleaning and gas freeing plans, risk assessments, records
Cleaning guidelines for expected cargoes and coating manufacturer's guidelines
Latest MEPC.2/Circular for approved cleaning agents
Observing a cleaning operation and mandatory prewash
ready: Written plan for each cleaning with cargo, SDS, risks, PPE, sequence, slops
Cleaning guidelines for all expected cargoes
Coating manufacturer's guidelines
Cargo Record Book entries
Additives stored per IMDG Code
traps: No procedure, or officer unfamiliar with P&A sections, guidelines or coating limits
Guidelines, coating guidelines or latest MEPC.2/Circular missing; written plans missing or not followed
Plan lacks cargo hazards, PPE, slops segregation or deck vapour control
No Responsible Officer supervision or crew briefing
Portable machines used but tank not treated as non-inert; steam into a tank that may be flammable
Additives not stored per IMDG, or other washing medium not covered in P&A Manual
say: We write a tank cleaning plan for every operation, covering the cargo and SDS, risks, PPE, method, slops and deck vapour control. The responsible officer supervises and briefs the crew first. We follow the P&A Manual, including mandatory prewash, and record everything.

practice.q: What is in a written tank cleaning plan?
a: Cargo, SDS and additives with hazards
Cleaning method and sequence, gas freeing
PPE, slops disposal and segregation
Keeping deck free from vapours

practice.q: Washing with portable machines: what atmosphere do you assume?
a: Treat the tank as non-inert
Overpressure of inert gas cannot be ensured
Air may enter and raise oxygen

tip: Hold the pre-cleaning meeting properly and note it, as the inspector looks for crew briefing evidence.

title: Chemical cargo compatibility charts
plain: Do officers know how to spot and separate incompatible cargoes when planning stowage?
why: Incompatible cargoes or vapours mixing can cause toxic gas, heat, fire or tank rupture.
checks: Company procedure for identifying and segregating incompatible cargoes
Compatibility chart in use with latest information
Current and previous stowage plans
Segregation means on deck such as spool pieces or spectacle flanges
Officer explains chart use and exceptions
ready: Procedure naming charts and segregation methods
Recognised chart with exception lists, latest version
Stowage plans marking incompatible pairs and how separated
Ship drawings showing segregation
P&A Manual
traps: No procedure, or officer cannot use the chart
No chart from a recognised authority, or it is out of date
Footnotes and cargo data sheets not checked; incompatible cargoes adjacent, without double barrier
Incompatible cargoes sharing a venting system
Tank cleaning after incompatible cargoes without mitigations in the plan
Segregation on deck differs from the stowage plan
say: We check every pair of cargoes against the compatibility chart and its exceptions, then check footnotes and data sheets. The stowage plan shows which cargoes are incompatible and how we separate them, covering tanks, pipelines, vents and drip trays.

practice.q: How do you separate incompatible cargoes?
a: Cofferdam, void space, pumproom, empty tank or compatible cargo between
Separate pumping, piping and venting
Spool pieces removed or double spectacle flanges

practice.q: What do you check besides the chart?
a: Chart footnotes and exceptions
Data sheets for both cargoes
Latest updated information

tip: Show the segregation on the stowage plan physically on deck, such as removed spool pieces, matching the plan.

title: Escape sets required by IBC Code
plain: Are there enough escape sets for everyone onboard, and do they protect breathing and eyes?
why: If cargo vapour escapes, everyone onboard needs to get out quickly and safely.
checks: Maintenance records for EEBDs in the maintenance plan
Two escape sets inspected at random: charged, marked, eye protection
Enough for everyone on board including visitors and contractors
Additional to SOLAS EEBDs in accommodation and machinery spaces
A rating explains location, purpose and use
ready: Escape sets for every person, at least 15 minutes duration
No filter-type sets
Marked as not for fire-fighting or cargo handling
Included in the company procedure and maintenance plan
Counted against the people onboard
traps: Duration under 15 minutes, or filter-type protection; no eye protection
Not marked 'not for fire-fighting or cargo handling'
Not additional to the SOLAS EEBDs; set not fully charged or not maintained per plan
Used for fire-fighting, cargo work or as the main means to enter bad atmospheres
Not enough sets for visitors, contractors, supernumeraries
Rating does not know where or how to use them
say: We carry escape sets for every person onboard, plus the SOLAS EEBDs. They give at least 15 minutes, with eye protection, no filters, and are marked not for fire-fighting or cargo work. They are inspected under the maintenance plan and the crew are trained.

practice.q: Rating: where is your escape set and how do you use it?
a: Know the location
Open it and don the hood or mask properly
Use only to escape, not to enter spaces

practice.q: Can you use the EEBD to enter a tank?
a: No, emergency escape only
Not for fire-fighting or cargo handling

tip: Count sets against the people list including visitors and contractors on the day.

title: Safety equipment required by the IBC Code
plain: Do officers know the procedures for IBC safety equipment including SCBAs, and is it ready for immediate use?

Spare air bottles or compressor arrangement
Monthly inspection logged and annual expert test
ready: Three complete sets stowed outside hazardous areas, marked, accessible
Fully charged cylinders and spares, straps slack
Monthly officer inspection in the logbook
Annual service by an expert, with training certificate if crew did it
Suits suitable for cargoes on the CoF and flammable atmospheres

Crew expert without manufacturer course certificate or special test equipment
say: We have the three complete IBC sets plus the SOLAS firefighting sets, stowed outside hazardous areas and marked. Cylinders are fully charged with spares, and straps are slack for quick donning. We inspect monthly, log it, and have an annual expert test.

practice.q: What is in one complete set?
a: Air-breathing apparatus, not stored oxygen
Protective clothing, boots, gloves, tight goggles
Fireproof lifeline and belt
Explosion-proof lamp

Crew member with manufacturer course within five years
Specialist test equipment onboard and certificate kept

Records of PPE inspections and inventory
PPE in storage and in use on deck
Chemical resistance list for the suits, suitable for flammable atmospheres
A deck officer or rating demonstrates selecting and donning a full set
ready: Procedure with PPE matrix by cargo and operation
Inventory and inspection records
SDS for cargoes handled
Chemical resistance list for suits
Suits, gloves, boots, head gear of matching resistance, in suitable sizes

Stored in an unsuitable place or in accommodation, in poor condition
No chemical resistance list or no flammable atmosphere evidence
Gloves or boots weaker than suit, not enough sizes; crew unfamiliar with donning a suit
say: Our procedure has a cargo-specific PPE matrix based on risk assessment and SDS. Crew are trained, a second person checks the suit before entry, and we manage time limits and fitness. Suits are cleaned, stored in a ventilated space, inspected and repaired or removed if defective.

practice.q: What eye protection at the manifold when disconnecting a hose?
a: Chemical splash goggles or spray hood
Face shields and safety spectacles are not suitable

practice.q: How do you check a suit before using it?

Second trained person checks it is worn correctly

title: Inert gas generator
plain: Do officers know how the IG generator works and is tested, and is it run and maintained as per maker and company?
why: The generator must reliably give inert gas to the design standard, or tanks lose their protection.
checks: Company procedures for IG generator and gas regulating valve
Plant in good order: no leaks, no pinholes or temporary repairs
Blowers free of excess vibration, spares if only one blower
Gas regulating and isolation valves working automatically or remotely
Records of inspection, testing and maintenance, and safe entry procedures posted
ready: Procedure for operation, inspection, testing, maintenance
Maker's instruction and maintenance manual
Inspection records with defects and rectification
Temperature and pressure sensors connected and reading sensibly
Entry procedure posted at the room matching the SMS
traps: No procedure, or officer unfamiliar; records missing or incomplete
Gas regulating or remote valves run on local control
Sensors disconnected or defective
Significant gas or liquid leaks, or excess blower vibration
One blower with insufficient spares; no positive pressure ventilation where required
Entry procedure missing, or not matching SMS (also affects 5.5.1)
say: Deck and engine departments work together to run the IG plant. We follow the maker's manual and company procedure for the generator and gas regulating valve, keep inspection and maintenance records including defects, and have entry procedures posted at the space.

practice.q: What does the IG plant do?
a: Supplies, cools, cleans, pressurises, monitors and controls inert gas delivery
Keeps inert gas within design criteria

practice.q: What would you check on a walk-round?

Blower vibration
Valves in automatic or remote, sensors working

tip: If entry procedures posted at the IG room differ from your SMS enclosed space procedure, you pick up a second observation.

title: Nitrogen generator inert gas system
plain: Do officers know how the nitrogen generator works and is tested, and is it run and maintained as per maker and company?
why: Nitrogen leaks cause oxygen deficiency and the waste gas is oxygen enriched, both serious hazards.
checks: Company procedure covering nitrogen generator and equipment
Compressor, air treatment, PSA or membrane units, receiver or buffer tank
Alarms: heater failure, low feed-air pressure, high air temperature, high condensate level
Extraction ventilation, safe entry procedure and asphyxiation warning signs
Officer explains hazards of nitrogen leaks and oxygen-enriched exhaust
ready: Procedure for operation, inspection, testing, maintenance
Maker's manual
Inspection and maintenance records including defects
Working visual and audible alarms
Warning signs for asphyxiation and for oxygen-enriched waste gas
traps: No procedure, or officer unfamiliar
Officer unaware of oxygen deficiency or oxygen-enriched exhaust dangers
Records missing or incomplete; any of the four alarms not working
Extraction ventilation not working in a dedicated compartment
No safe entry procedure at the entrance; equipment defective in any respect
Entry procedure not matching SMS (also affects 5.5.1)
say: We run the nitrogen generator per the maker's manual and our procedure, with records of inspection and maintenance. I know the two main dangers: oxygen deficiency from nitrogen leaks, and oxygen-enriched waste gas. Warning signs are posted, and the extraction ventilation and alarms are tested.

practice.q: What dangers does the nitrogen generator bring?
a: Nitrogen leak makes an oxygen-deficient atmosphere
Waste gas contains over 23.5 percent oxygen
Oil with oxygen-enriched air can react violently

practice.q: Which alarms must work?
a: Electric heater failure, if fitted
Low feed-air pressure or flow
High air temperature
High condensate level at water separator drain

tip: Test the four alarms before the inspector asks, since any inoperative alarm is a negative.
